subject: Business Management
distinctive: Business management sits in the guide's individuals and societies group, so your essay explores a question connected to human experience and behaviour. The guide's business management examples each focus on one real organisation: one essay examines how McDonald's trains its managers, and another examines McDonald's relationship with its charity, Ronald McDonald House Charities. The guide's sport example also points to a case study: a brand sponsoring a football club.

The guide says that content alone does not make an essay a business management essay. The concepts, methods and theories of business management are what give you insight and let you build a well-constructed argument. The same broad interest, such as sport, could become a business management essay or a global politics essay depending on the approach you take.

The guide's aims for the whole group apply to business management too. An individuals and societies essay lets you challenge assumptions about the social world, increase your knowledge by exploring the subject literature, and select theories or concepts and apply suitable methodologies to formulate an argument.

sources.primary: Primary research means data you collect yourself, such as interviews and surveys. In the guide's Hamburger University example, the student interviews trainers and surveys graduates. Primary research is not required in every business management essay: the guide's second example uses secondary data only.
sources.secondary: Every extended essay must include secondary research (a literature review). In the guide's examples, secondary sources are used to describe and evaluate McDonald's training courses, and recently published academic articles about Ronald McDonald House Charities supply the evidence for the second essay.

methods: Case study of one organisation: the guide's sport example is to analyse a case study of a brand sponsoring a football club.
Describe and evaluate one practice of an organisation using secondary sources, supported by findings from your own primary research.
Primary research through interviews with people who carry out the practice and surveys of people who experienced the practice, as in the Hamburger University example.
Secondary data only: weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of a business relationship, as in the Ronald McDonald House Charities example.

The guide lists further research strategies for all individuals and societies subjects: comparisons, case studies, discourse analysis, critical analysis of a theory or concept, and in-depth analysis of a primary source.
choosing_topic: Your topic can come from your own life experience, from an issue of contemporary debate, from a topic in one of your favourite subjects, or from a topic related to but not covered by a favourite subject.
Big real-world issues, such as the future of global capitalism, can work if you pose the issue as a well-focused question explored from the perspective of business management.

Your topic must be considered in terms of one individuals and societies subject. A broad interest such as sport could be written up in several subjects; the business management version in the guide analyses a brand sponsoring a football club.
Choose your angle for the approach, not the content. The concepts, methods and theories of business management are what ground your topic in business management.

examples.topic: How McDonald’s trains its managers in the USA: The Hamburger University in Chicago
examples.rq: To what extent is McDonald’s Hamburger University an optimal form of training?
examples.why: The essay describes and evaluates McDonald's in-house training courses using secondary sources. Findings from primary research support the evaluation: interviews with trainers who work at Hamburger University and surveys of graduates of Hamburger University.

examples.topic: McDonald’s charitable work: Ronald McDonald House Charities (RMHC)
examples.rq: Who benefits more from the relationship: RMHC or McDonald’s?
examples.why: Many recent academic articles discuss RMHC, some praising the charity and some criticising it on the grounds that donations could be more substantial. Using secondary data only, the essay discusses the advantages and disadvantages of the relationship between McDonald's and RMHC.

structure: Make your research question and your research methods align clearly with business management. The guide suggests checking the business management subject guide to confirm you understand the nature of the subject and its methodology.
Keep your line of argument within the logic of business management: use the subject's terminology and follow its style and structural conventions.
In the Hamburger University example, secondary sources carry the description and evaluation, and primary research findings support that evaluation.
Clearly label diagrams, images and graphs, acknowledge any that are the work of others, and refer to each one actively in the body of your essay.
Use headings to organise your essay where appropriate.
pitfalls: Relying on content alone. Without business management concepts, methods and theories, your essay will not be grounded in business management.
A research question or research methods that do not clearly align with business management.
Writing without business management terminology. The guide says that using the subject's terminology identifies you as someone who understands the subject.
A one-sided discussion. The guide says a balanced discussion considers different perspectives on your topic, and your evaluation should weigh up the strengths and limitations of your essay.
Using sources or methods without checking that they suit business management. The guide advises asking your supervisor and reading the business management subject guide.
Diagrams or graphs that are unlabelled, unacknowledged, or never referred to in the body of your essay.
rules: Your essay must include secondary research (a literature review).
Your topic must be considered in terms of business management, even if the same topic could be approached from another individuals and societies subject.
think: Which single real organisation is at the centre of your idea, and can you name the organisation now?
Which business management concepts or theories would you use to analyse the organisation's practice or decision?
Could secondary sources alone answer your research question, or would interviews or surveys with people inside the organisation give you evidence you cannot find elsewhere?
If you removed the business management concepts from your idea, would your question turn into an economics or global politics question instead?
Whose perspectives on the organisation's practice would a balanced discussion need to include?

subject: Economics
distinctive: Economics sits in the guide's individuals and societies group, so your essay explores a question connected to human experience and behaviour. The guide's two economics examples share one pattern: an economic theory or idea is set against evidence. One essay tests the neoclassical argument about minimum wages against current research, and the other evaluates how far mobile banking has contributed to economic development in one town or village.

The guide says that content alone does not make an essay an economics essay. The concepts, methods and theories of economics are what give you insight and let you build a well-constructed argument. The guide's own example of economics terminology is “supply and demand”: using terms like “supply and demand” in a meaningful, explanatory way shows that you understand the subject.

The guide says individuals and societies subjects can tackle big questions about our shared present, past and future, and names the future of global capitalism as one such real-world issue. An economics essay turns a big issue into a well-focused question explored from the perspective of economics.

sources.primary: Primary research means data you collect yourself, such as surveys, interviews or local prices. In the guide's mobile banking example, primary research in one town or village is used to judge how far economic development has happened there. Not every economics essay needs it: the guide's minimum wage example uses published research only.
sources.secondary: Every extended essay must include secondary research (a literature review). The guide's minimum wage example researches the neoclassical argument and the studies behind the counterarguments, and the mobile banking example includes data that other researchers obtained through randomised control trials.

methods: Test an economic theory against current research: present the theory, then research the counterarguments and evaluate them by the nature of their evidence and the studies carried out.
Use recent evidence from news articles or data banks to assess a link between two variables, such as minimum wages and unemployment, in different places.
Combine primary research in one place with data that other researchers obtained through randomised control trials, then evaluate how far an outcome such as economic development has occurred.

The guide lists further research strategies for all individuals and societies subjects: comparisons, case studies, discourse analysis, critical analysis of a theory or concept, and in-depth analysis of a primary source.
choosing_topic: Your topic can come from your own life experience, from an issue of contemporary debate, from a topic in one of your favourite subjects, or from a topic related to but not covered by a favourite subject.

Big real-world issues, such as the future of global capitalism or the environmental and climatic crisis, can work if you pose the issue as a well-focused question explored from the perspective of economics.
Your topic must be considered in terms of one individuals and societies subject, even though many topics could be approached from more than one subject in the group.
Choose your angle for the approach, not the content. The concepts, methods and theories of economics are what ground your topic in economics.
The guide's economics examples narrow their focus with a named theory (the neoclassical argument about minimum wages) or a named place and start date (town or village “X” since 2010).

examples.rq: Does current economic research into minimum wage invalidate the neoclassical argument that increasing the minimum wage will lead to increased levels of unemployment?
examples.why: Neoclassical economics argues that raising the minimum wage raises unemployment, while newer research argues that the neoclassical argument rests on flawed assumptions. The essay presents the neoclassical argument, then evaluates the counterarguments by the nature of their evidence and studies. Recent evidence from news articles or data banks can test the link between minimum wages and unemployment in different places, and a conclusion at each point of analysis builds towards a judgement on how valid the neoclassical model is.

examples.topic: The role of mobile banking in economic development
examples.rq: How has increased access to mobile banking contributed to economic development in town (or village) “X” since 2010?
examples.why: The essay researches how mobile banking can contribute to economic development in theory, including data that other researchers obtained through randomised control trials. The essay focuses on aspects of development such as higher incomes, health and education outcomes, the empowerment of women and civic participation. Primary research then leads to an evaluation of how far economic development has occurred in the area investigated.

structure: Make your research question and your research methods align clearly with economics. The guide suggests checking the economics subject guide to confirm you understand the nature of the subject and its methodology.
Build your argument in stages. In the guide's minimum wage example, each independent point of analysis ends with a conclusion, and those conclusions build towards the overall judgement.
Keep your line of argument within the logic of economics: use terminology such as “supply and demand” and follow the subject's style and structural conventions.
Clearly label diagrams and graphs, acknowledge any that are the work of others, and refer to each one actively in the body of your essay.
Use headings to organise your essay where appropriate.
pitfalls: Relying on content alone. Without economics concepts, methods and theories, your essay will not be grounded in economics.
A research question or research methods that do not clearly align with economics.
Reporting studies without evaluating them. In the guide's minimum wage example, each counterargument is judged by the nature of its evidence and the studies carried out.
A one-sided discussion. The guide says a balanced discussion considers different perspectives on your topic, and your evaluation should weigh up the strengths and limitations of your essay.
Using economics terms as labels only. The guide asks you to use key concepts in a meaningful and explanatory way.
Diagrams or graphs that are unlabelled, unacknowledged, or never referred to in the body of your essay.
rules: Your essay must include secondary research (a literature review).
Your topic must be considered in terms of economics, even if the same topic could be approached from another individuals and societies subject.
think: Which economic theory or model does your idea test, and can you state the model's prediction in one sentence?
What evidence could confirm or challenge that prediction: published studies, data banks, news articles, or your own primary research?
Can you limit your research question to one place and a clear time period, as the mobile banking example does with town “X” since 2010?
Which economics terms would you need in order to explain your analysis, and could you use each term to explain something rather than just name it?
Which economists or studies disagree with the theory you are testing, and how would you judge the quality of their evidence?
If you took the economic theory out of your idea, would your question become a geography or global politics question instead?

subject: Global Politics
distinctive: Global politics sits in the guide's individuals and societies group, so your essay explores a question connected to human experience and behaviour. The guide's two global politics examples follow one pattern: a literature review of key political concepts, such as power, conflict or the right to privacy, then analysis of one or more real cases, then an evaluation that links the facts of each case with the theories.

The guide says that in global politics, relevant academic secondary sources substantiate your line of argument, and primary data collected through appropriate methods may or may not be added. Content alone does not make an essay a global politics essay: the concepts, methods and theories of global politics are what let you build a well-constructed argument.

The guide's sport example shows the global politics angle on a broad interest: exploring global discourses around women in sports and how those discourses influence political decisions about gender rights. The guide also names migration and governance in a digital age as real-world issues for the group.

sources.primary: Primary data is optional in global politics: academic secondary sources carry your argument, and you may add primary data collected with appropriate methods. For example, the guide's Snapchat example analyses the app's own privacy policy and the personal data the app needs.
sources.secondary: Relevant academic secondary sources substantiate your line of argument, and every extended essay must include secondary research (a literature review). Both global politics examples in the guide open with a literature review of the key concepts.

methods: Literature review of key political concepts, for example power, conflict, terrorism, leadership, feminism in politics and soft power, to build the framework for your analysis.
Comparison of cases in two countries, as in the example comparing responses to terrorist attacks in New Zealand and France.
Analysis of one case through the documents the case produces, as in the example analysing Snapchat's data requirements and privacy policy.
Discourse analysis: the guide's sport example explores global discourses around women in sports.
The guide lists further research strategies for all individuals and societies subjects: case studies, critical analysis of a theory or concept, and in-depth analysis of a primary source.
choosing_topic: Your topic can come from your own life experience, from an issue of contemporary debate, from a topic in one of your favourite subjects, or from a topic related to but not covered by a favourite subject.

Big real-world issues, such as migration, governance in a digital age or the environmental and climatic crisis, can work if you pose the issue as a well-focused question explored from the perspective of global politics.

Your topic must be considered in terms of one individuals and societies subject. A broad interest such as sport could be written up in several subjects; the global politics version in the guide explores discourses around women in sports and political decisions about gender rights.
Choose your angle for the approach, not the content. The concepts, methods and theories of global politics are what ground your topic in global politics.
Both global politics research questions in the guide name the case inside the question: New Zealand and France in one, Snapchat in the European Union in the other.

examples.rq: To what extent is female leadership better at facing conflict? Responses to terrorist attacks in New Zealand and France.
examples.why: The essay opens with a literature review of the concepts of power, conflict, terrorism, leadership, feminism in politics and soft power. The essay then analyses terrorist attacks and the responses to them in New Zealand under Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and in France under President Emmanuel Macron. An evaluation of both situations reaches a conclusion that links facts with theories.

examples.topic: Big data, apps and human rights
examples.rq: To what extent is the large amount of personal data collected by mobile apps a breach of the right to privacy? The case of Snapchat in the European Union (EU).
examples.why: The essay reviews the literature on big data, human rights, universalism, interdependence, indivisibility, the right to privacy and data protection. The essay then analyses the personal data needed to download and use Snapchat, and Snapchat's privacy policy. The facts are linked with the key concepts to develop an argument and a conclusion that answers the research question.

structure: The guide's global politics examples move in three stages: a literature review of key concepts, analysis of the case or cases, and an evaluation that links the facts with the theories.

Make your research question and your research methods align clearly with global politics. The guide suggests checking the global politics subject guide to confirm you understand the nature of the subject and its methodology.
Keep your line of argument within the logic of global politics: use the subject's terminology and follow its style and structural conventions.

Clearly label diagrams, images, graphs and maps (with all required elements, such as a scale and a key or legend), acknowledge any that are the work of others, and refer to each one actively in the body of your essay.
Use headings to organise your essay where appropriate.
pitfalls: Relying on content alone. Without global politics concepts, methods and theories, your essay will not be grounded in global politics.
Keeping facts and theories apart. Both guide examples end by linking the facts of the case to the concepts from the literature review.
A research question or research methods that do not clearly align with global politics.
A one-sided discussion. The guide says a balanced discussion considers different perspectives on your topic, and your evaluation should weigh up the strengths and limitations of your essay.
Using key concepts without applying them. The guide says applying key concepts in your writing is essential.
Maps, diagrams or graphs that are unlabelled, missing a scale or key, unacknowledged, or never referred to in the body of your essay.
rules: Your essay must include secondary research (a literature review).
Your topic must be considered in terms of global politics, even if the same topic could be approached from another individuals and societies subject.
think: Which political concepts, such as power, conflict, human rights or soft power, would your literature review need to define?
Which one or two real cases would you analyse, and can you name each case inside your research question?
If you compare two cases, are the cases similar enough that a difference between them tells you something about your concept?
Can academic secondary sources carry your argument, or is there a document, such as a policy, that you would need to analyse yourself?
How will your conclusion link the facts of your case back to the theories in your literature review?
Whose perspectives on your case would a balanced discussion need to include?
